definition: Greek for “remembrance” or “memorial.” The Eucharist is an anamnesis: not a mere mental recollection but a memorial sacrifice that makes Christ’s offering truly present.

The Greek verb in Matthew 6:7, usually translated “babble” or “heap up empty phrases.” Jesus condemns pagan babbling in prayer — not repetition itself, which Scripture uses constantly (see the Psalms, Revelation 4:8).
St. Augustine’s spiritual autobiography (c. 400) — the classic story of a brilliant sinner’s conversion, and one of the most influential books in Christian history.
Latin for “Word of God.” Vatican II’s Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation (1965): Scripture and Tradition flow from a single divine source and are interpreted by the Church’s Magisterium.
Latin for “On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.” St. Augustine’s commentary urging a careful, non-literalistic reading of the creation accounts where reason and evidence warrant it.
The honor and veneration given to the saints — deep reverence, but not worship. See also Latria and Hyperdulia.
Hebrew for “servant.” The “Servant of the Lord” (ebed YHWH) in Isaiah’s Servant Songs, which Christians read as pointing to Christ.
Greek for “I am.” Jesus’s words in John 8:58 (“Before Abraham was, I AM”), echoing God’s name in Exodus 3:14 — a direct claim to divinity, which is why his hearers picked up stones.
Latin for “faith formed by charity.” The Catholic understanding of saving faith: faith working through love (Galatians 5:6) — not mere intellectual assent.
Hebrew for “Great Lady” or “Queen Mother.” In the Davidic kingdom the king’s mother held a formal office of intercessor — the biblical pattern for Mary’s queenship.
Hebrew for “devoted” or “banned.” The Old Testament practice of consecrating something to God through total destruction, as in the conquest narratives (Deuteronomy 7, Joshua 6).
Greek for “of the same substance.” The key word of the Nicene Creed: the Son is homoousios with the Father — fully God, not a creature, however exalted.
Latin for “Of the Human Race.” Pope Pius XII’s 1950 encyclical addressing theology and science, including the Church’s guidance on evolution.
“Higher veneration.” The special honor given to Mary alone — above the saints (dulia) but infinitely below the adoration owed to God (latria).
Latin for “image of God.” Humanity is created in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) — the foundation of Catholic teaching on human dignity.
Latin for “in the person of Christ.” In celebrating the sacraments — above all the Eucharist — the priest acts in the very person of Christ, not merely as his representative.
Latin for “the sheer act of being itself.” St. Thomas Aquinas’s description of God: not a being among beings, but Being itself, with no potential unrealized.
Greek for “Lord.” The title used for God in the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) — and applied to Jesus throughout the New Testament, identifying him with the God of Israel.
The adoration owed to God alone — total, absolute worship. Catholics distinguish it sharply from dulia (veneration of saints) and hyperdulia (Mary’s special honor).
C. S. Lewis’s classic (1952) arguing for the core of Christian belief — famous for the moral argument for God and the “liar, lunatic, or Lord” trilemma about Jesus.
Latin for “The most bountiful God.” Pope Pius XII’s 1950 apostolic constitution solemnly defining the Assumption of Mary as dogma.
Greek for “flesh.” As in “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) — the scandal and glory of the Incarnation.
Latin for “of one’s own right.” A self-governing Church in Catholicism: each Eastern Catholic Church is sui iuris — with its own liturgy, law, and hierarchy — while in full communion with Rome.
Shorthand for the Summa Theologiae (see below) — St. Thomas Aquinas’s great systematic theology.
Latin for “Summary of Theology.” St. Thomas Aquinas’s masterwork (c. 1265–1274): the classic systematic presentation of Catholic doctrine in objections, answers, and replies.

Greek for “God-bearer,” translated “Mother of God.” Defined at the Council of Ephesus (431): because Jesus is one divine Person, Mary is truly the mother of God the Son — a title about Christ’s divinity, not Mary’s.
Greek for “God.” The word at the center of the John 1:1 debate: “the Word was theos” — God, not “a god.”
Greek for “to chew” or “gnaw.” The deliberately graphic word Jesus uses in John 6 (“whoever chews my flesh”) — a strong support for the realistic, Eucharistic reading of the passage.
Latin for “Restoration of Unity.” Vatican II’s Decree on Ecumenism (1964), setting out the Catholic approach to relations with other Christians.
Hebrew for “memorial.” The Passover’s zikkaron — a remembrance that makes the past event present to those celebrating it — is the Jewish background to the Eucharistic anamnesis.
